docs.text: This course is designed to bring learners up to the level of the Autodesk Certified User in Revit for Architectural Design. The ACU is the entry-level Autodesk Revit certification. The next step after this is the Autodesk Certified Professional in Revit for Architectural Design, which assumes a much deeper level of project experience. The ACU level is best understood as the minimum practical knowledge needed to operate Revit safely and efficiently in a project environment. It does not make someone an expert, but it should give them enough confidence to understand the interface, model basic architectural elements, create views, annotate drawings, produce sheets, and recognise where to look when they need help. Some ACU preparation courses are delivered intensively over two or three days. This programme stretches the same foundation over approximately two months so that learners can practise between sessions, connect the topics to live office work, and absorb the ideas at a more realistic pace. At the end of the course, learners should be in a position to attempt an online certification test if they want formal evidence of their knowledge. In practice, the real learning continues on live projects. Revit takes time and repetition: the aim is to remember the core concepts from the lessons, know what to look up, and become comfortable using Autodesk Help and project standards when new situations appear. docs.text: Goal ¶ Understand the Revit workspace, open a project, navigate views, and recognise the main tools used during a basic modelling session. Prerequisites ¶ Autodesk Revit installed Download the Lesson 01 exercise file A sample project or Revit default template Key Concepts ¶ BIM vs CAD MacLeamy Curve Project Browser Properties Palette Ribbon tools View controls 3D navigation Selection and modification tools Basic digital literacy for opening, saving, and finding files BIM vs CAD ¶ Introduce Revit as a coordinated BIM model rather than a set of disconnected CAD drawings. Show how plans, sections, elevations, schedules, and sheets all read from the same project model. One of the most important ideas in Revit is that the project behaves like a central database. A wall is not just a line in plan; it is an object with height, type, material, fire rating, location, and relationships to levels, rooms, views, schedules, and sheets. When that object changes, every view that depends on it can update from the same underlying information. For example, imagine you prepare facade visualisations. In a less coordinated workflow, you might export geometry from Revit, adjust it in Rhino, assign materials, and send it to D5 or another visualisation tool. If the facade geometry or material changes later, those changes may happen outside Revit. In your team, the technical coordinator then needs to update drawings or schedules separately, and the facade coordinator needs to check whether the facade information still matches. The team can quickly end up with several versions of the same building. In a Revit-based BIM workflow, you make the relevant geometry and material changes in the live project model where possible. Plans, sections, elevations, schedules, and sheets can then read the updated information from the same place. If the model is linked into D5 or another visualisation workflow, the visualisation is based on current coordinated geometry, reducing the risk that material assignments or design changes are lost during export. MacLeamy Curve ¶ The MacLeamy Curve is a useful way to explain why BIM changes the design process. It compares the ability to influence project outcomes, the cost of making changes, and where design effort usually happens. Source: DDG Global, "MacLeamy Curve - How BIM affects the design process" . The key lesson for Revit users is that BIM rewards earlier thinking. Coordinated models, shared information, and earlier collaboration help teams make important decisions while they are still relatively cheap and easy to change. Then orient learners around the interface: Ribbon tabs and panels Quick Access Toolbar Properties Palette Project Browser View Control Bar Status Bar Exercise ¶ Open Revit and create a new architectural project. Discuss where Revit shifts effort compared with a traditional drawing-led workflow. Find the Project Browser and Properties Palette. Open a floor plan, elevation, section, and 3D view. Practice zooming, panning, orbiting, and switching between views. Select model elements using click, window selection, tab select, and filters. Use move, copy, rotate, and temporary hide/isolate. Try trim/extend, align, offset, mirror, split, array, scale, pin/unpin, and copy/paste aligned on prepared elements. Save the project locally. Checklist ¶ [ ] I can create or open a Revit project. [ ] I can explain why BIM shifts design decisions earlier in the project. [ ] I can identify the main interface areas. [ ] I can switch between common view types. [ ] I can navigate a model in 2D and 3D. [ ] I can select and modify basic elements. [ ] I can use the core Modify tools listed in the ACU objectives. Homework ¶ Practice navigation shortcuts. Open and explore sample projects. Duplicate a view and rename it clearly. Revit Help Links ¶ Revit user interface Project Browser Navigate views Editing Elements Keyboard shortcuts

docs.text: Goal ¶ Set up the primary datum structure of a Revit project and understand how levels, grids, and views relate to each other. Prerequisites ¶ Session 01 completed A new or sample architectural project Basic view navigation confidence Key Concepts ¶ Datum elements Levels and associated views Grids and structural reference systems Architectural columns on grids Structural columns and coordination intent Basic wall placement from grid references Datum extents Naming consistency View organisation Demonstration ¶ Explain levels as the vertical control system of the project. Show how building elements can be hosted or constrained to levels, and how renaming a level can also rename the associated plan view. Then introduce grids as the project reference system used for coordination, dimensioning, and setting out. Show bubble visibility, extents, grid names, and how datum visibility can differ between views. Place architectural columns on grid intersections so learners understand the exam link between grids and columns. Architectural and Structural Columns ¶ Revit has both architectural columns and structural columns. They can look similar in a beginner model, but they carry different meaning and are used for different coordination workflows. Architectural columns are normally used where the column is part of the architectural definition of the space. They may represent a visible finish, casing, boxing-out, pilaster, or column enclosure. They belong to the architectural model and are often useful when the architect needs to control what is seen in plans, sections, elevations, and room layouts. Structural columns are used when the element represents a load-bearing structural member. They belong to the structural modelling logic and are usually coordinated with the structural engineer. Structural columns have structural behaviour, analytical relevance, and category settings that support structural documentation and coordination. In practice, an architectural model may show columns for spatial and visual coordination while the structural model contains the authoritative structural columns. In a live project, do not duplicate structural information casually. Agree with the project team whether the architect should model architectural column finishes, structural column placeholders, or rely on linked structural models. For this training session, place architectural columns on grid intersections to understand the grid-and-column relationship without introducing full structural modelling. The main lesson is that grids provide a shared reference system, and columns often make that reference system visible in the building layout. Basic Wall Layout From Grids ¶ This session also introduces simple wall placement so learners can see why levels and grids matter. The aim is not yet to understand wall build-ups, layers, materials, or detailed wall types. That comes in the next session. For now, use walls as simple layout elements: Draw external walls using grids as setting-out references. Set the wall base and top constraints to the correct levels. Use the location line to decide whether the wall is placed by centreline, finish face, or core face. Use temporary dimensions and Align to keep walls coordinated with grids. Keep the layout simple enough that the datum structure remains the main focus. By the end of this session, learners should understand that levels control vertical relationships, grids control setting-out, and walls are easier to manage when they are placed against a clear datum strategy. Project Positioning ¶ Revit projects also need a clear positioning strategy. Even in a small training model, learners should understand that the building has an internal coordinate system and that real projects often need to relate to survey, site, and linked consultant models. The three key reference concepts are: Internal Origin: Revit's fixed internal reference point. It should be treated as the stable mathematical origin of the model. Project Base Point: the project team's local reference point. It is often used for a meaningful project coordinate such as a setting-out point or agreed local datum. Survey Point: the relationship between the Revit project and a real-world survey coordinate system. For this training course, keep the model close to the internal origin and avoid moving the building very far away. Revit has distance limits, and modelling too far from the internal origin can cause display, snapping, accuracy, and coordination problems. In practice, the team should decide the coordinate strategy at the start of a project rather than after models have already been built. For now, the exercise is conceptual: identify the project base point, survey point, and internal origin, but do not change the project coordinates unless instructed. Exercise ¶ Open an elevation view. Create a set of building levels. Rename levels and confirm associated view names. Add grids to a floor plan. Adjust grid bubbles and datum extents. Rename grid bubbles. Create plan views for the required levels using View > Plan Views > Floor Plan . Check that each plan view is named clearly and appears in the correct Project Browser location. Place architectural columns on selected grid intersections and discuss how this differs from placing structural columns. Draw a simple external wall layout using the grids as setting-out references. Set wall base and top constraints so the walls relate correctly to the levels. Use Align and temporary dimensions to coordinate wall positions with grids. Align levels and grids so the datum lines read clearly in elevations and plans. Adjust 2D and 3D extents where needed so the documentation is tidy. Create a scope box around the main building area and assign it to relevant plan views. Use it to keep crop regions and datum extents consistent. Identify the internal origin, project base point, and survey point. Review the Project Browser, rename any unclear views, and remove or ignore duplicate views that are not needed for the exercise. Checklist ¶ [ ] I can create and rename levels. [ ] I understand that levels can generate plan views. [ ] I can place and adjust grids. [ ] I can control datum visibility and extents. [ ] I can explain the difference between architectural and structural columns. [ ] I can place architectural columns on a grid. [ ] I can create plan views for levels. [ ] I can use a scope box to coordinate view crops and datum extents. [ ] I can create a simple wall layout using grids as references. [ ] I can constrain simple walls between levels. [ ] I can describe the internal origin, project base point, and survey point. [ ] I can keep view names and datum names consistent. Homework ¶ Recreate a simple structural grid layout. Add three levels to a fresh project and name them clearly. docs.text: Goal ¶ Model a simple floor plan using walls, doors, and windows while understanding hosted elements and type versus instance properties. Prerequisites ¶ Session 02 completed Project levels and grids available Basic selection and modification confidence Key Concepts ¶ Architectural walls Wall location lines Base and top constraints Wall joins Hosted doors and windows Wall and shaft openings Type properties Instance properties Demonstration ¶ Show how walls are constrained between levels and how their location line affects placement accuracy. Demonstrate wall joins, temporary dimensions, and basic wall type changes. Then place doors and windows into walls. Explain hosted behaviour, level placement, flip controls, sill heights, head heights, and why deleting a host wall affects hosted components. Demonstrate wall openings and shaft openings as separate opening tools. This session uses a small amount of loaded content so learners understand the normal Revit workflow for doors and windows. The focus is still on placing and controlling hosted elements, not on building a full family library. Session 10 will look more closely at where to find appropriate models and families, including office libraries, manufacturer content, and reliable external sources. Session 11 will then introduce the basics of editing and creating families so learners understand how custom content is made. Wall Types and Compound Structure ¶ Walls are system families. This means they are created and edited inside the project rather than loaded as separate .rfa files. To create a new wall type, duplicate an existing wall type, rename it clearly, and edit its type properties. The most important setting is the compound structure. A compound wall is built from layers, and each layer can have a function, material, thickness, and position relative to the core. Typical layer functions include structure, substrate, thermal or air layer, finish, and membrane. Revit uses these layer functions when joining walls, dimensioning to core faces, and representing walls in different levels of detail. Wall location line controls where the wall is placed relative to the line you draw. For example, a wall can be placed by centreline, core centreline, finish face, or core face. This matters when setting out walls from grids, boundaries, or existing geometry. Wall joins control how walls clean up where they meet. Good wall joins make drawings readable, but they should still be checked in plan and section. Where the automatic join is not appropriate, edit the join condition rather than drawing over it with 2D lines. Also be aware of related wall tools: Wall sweeps add continuous profiles such as skirtings, copings, or bands. Wall reveals cut continuous recesses into walls. Stacked walls combine different wall types vertically, for example a plinth wall below a different upper wall type. Curtain Walls ¶ Curtain walls are a special wall system used for glazed facades, screens, storefronts, and panelised wall assemblies. They are still part of the wall toolset, but they introduce grids, mullions, panels, and different editing behaviour. For the Autodesk Certified User level, learners should recognise that curtain walls exist and understand that they are not the same as ordinary basic walls. This session can show a short demonstration only: place a simple curtain wall type, add or adjust curtain grids, and point out mullions and panels. Detailed facade design, custom panels, and advanced curtain wall workflows should sit later in the course or in project-specific training. Exercise ¶ Create a simple rectangular floor plan. Add internal partitions. Adjust wall constraints and location lines. Review wall build-up, type properties, and how changing a wall type differs from moving or constraining a wall instance. Duplicate a wall type, rename it, and edit its compound structure. Change the wall location line and compare the placement result. Review wall joins at corners and intersections. Briefly place a curtain wall type and identify curtain grids, mullions, and panels. Place doors in internal and external walls. Place windows and adjust sill heights. Review head height and placement level. Use flip controls to correct orientation. Load a new window family, such as a sash window, using Insert > Load Family . Choose a suitable family from the Revit online library. Place the loaded sash window into an external wall and adjust its sill height, type, and position. Create a wall opening and a shaft opening. Modify one wall type and compare type and instance changes. Checklist ¶ [ ] I can draw walls accurately. [ ] I can set base and top constraints. [ ] I can identify where wall type build-up is edited. [ ] I can duplicate a wall type and edit its compound structure. [ ] I can explain wall location line and wall joins. [ ] I recognise curtain walls as a special wall system. [ ] I can place hosted doors and windows. [ ] I can load a new door or window family into the project. [ ] I can use flip controls. [ ] I can create wall and shaft openings. [ ] I understand type versus instance changes. Homework ¶ Create variations of wall types. Model a small room layout with at least two doors and four windows. Place a simple curtain wall and identify one panel and one mullion. docs.text: Walls are system families. This means they are created and edited inside the project rather than loaded as separate .rfa files. To create a new wall type, duplicate an existing wall type, rename it clearly, and edit its type properties. The most important setting is the compound structure. A compound wall is built from layers, and each layer can have a function, material, thickness, and position relative to the core. Typical layer functions include structure, substrate, thermal or air layer, finish, and membrane. Revit uses these layer functions when joining walls, dimensioning to core faces, and representing walls in different levels of detail. Wall location line controls where the wall is placed relative to the line you draw. For example, a wall can be placed by centreline, core centreline, finish face, or core face. This matters when setting out walls from grids, boundaries, or existing geometry. Wall joins control how walls clean up where they meet. Good wall joins make drawings readable, but they should still be checked in plan and section. Where the automatic join is not appropriate, edit the join condition rather than drawing over it with 2D lines. Also be aware of related wall tools: Wall sweeps add continuous profiles such as skirtings, copings, or bands. Wall reveals cut continuous recesses into walls. Stacked walls combine different wall types vertically, for example a plinth wall below a different upper wall type.

docs.text: Curtain walls are a special wall system used for glazed facades, screens, storefronts, and panelised wall assemblies. They are still part of the wall toolset, but they introduce grids, mullions, panels, and different editing behaviour. For the Autodesk Certified User level, learners should recognise that curtain walls exist and understand that they are not the same as ordinary basic walls. This session can show a short demonstration only: place a simple curtain wall type, add or adjust curtain grids, and point out mullions and panels. Detailed facade design, custom panels, and advanced curtain wall workflows should sit later in the course or in project-specific training.

docs.text: Goal ¶ Control how the model appears in different views and troubleshoot common visibility problems. Prerequisites ¶ Sessions 01-04 completed A model containing walls, doors, windows, floors, roofs, and ceilings Key Concepts ¶ Visibility/Graphics overrides Category visibility Temporary hide/isolate Detail level Visual styles Crop regions View templates Categories, families, types, and instances View range Underlays 3D section boxes Camera views Demonstration ¶ Explain that Revit views are controlled by view-specific settings. Show the hierarchy from category-level visibility to element-level overrides, temporary hide/isolate, and view templates. Demonstrate common visibility issues and a systematic troubleshooting process covering hidden elements, reveal hidden elements, category overrides, underlays, view range, phases, discipline settings, and linked model visibility. Categories, Families, Types, and Instances ¶ Visibility control in Revit makes much more sense once learners understand the hierarchy of categories, families, types, and instances. Categories are the broad built-in groups that Revit uses to organise model and annotation elements. Examples include Walls, Doors, Windows, Floors, Furniture, Generic Models, Rooms, and Dimensions. Categories are not created casually by users; they are part of Revit's structure. They control many important behaviours, including Visibility/Graphics, Object Styles, tags, schedules, filters, cut behaviour, and which tools can create or edit an element. Families sit inside categories. A door family belongs to the Doors category, a chair family belongs to the Furniture category, and a window family belongs to the Windows category. The category tells Revit how the object behaves at a high level; the family defines the actual geometry, parameters, and rules for a particular object. Types are variations within a family. For example, one window family might contain several types with different widths, heights, frame arrangements, or materials. Changing a type affects every instance using that type unless a value is instance-specific. Instances are the individual placed objects in the model. One placed door in one wall is an instance. It belongs to a family, uses a type, and is governed by a category. Instance properties control things that can vary from one placed object to another, such as sill height, mark, comments, or location. This hierarchy is one of the first checks when troubleshooting visibility: If every door is hidden, check the Doors category in Visibility/Graphics. If one door family looks wrong, check the family or type settings. If one placed door is wrong, check the instance properties or whether that instance has been hidden or overridden in the view. If an object cannot be tagged or scheduled as expected, check whether it is in the correct category. Source reference: Cosmere Technologies, "Revit Family Types" . Exercise ¶ Duplicate a floor plan as a working view. Adjust detail level and visual style. Use Visibility/Graphics overrides. Temporarily hide and isolate elements. Select a door, window, wall, and furniture object and identify each element's category, family, type, and instance properties. Hide one category through Visibility/Graphics, then restore it. Hide one individual element, then use Reveal Hidden Elements to find it again. Create a simple view template. Apply the template to a second view. Duplicate views using Duplicate, Duplicate with Detailing, and Duplicate as Dependent. Create a 3D view and modify a section box boundary. Create a camera view. Add an underlay to a plan view and use it to compare geometry from another level. Create a plan region where a local area needs a different view range. Diagnose prepared visibility issues. View Range ¶ View range controls the vertical slice of the model that appears in a plan view. It is one of the most common reasons why elements appear, disappear, or display differently from what learners expect. The key settings are: Top: the upper limit of the main view range. Cut Plane: the height where Revit cuts through model elements. Bottom: the lower limit of the main view range. View Depth: the additional depth Revit can look beyond the bottom of the primary range. For a normal floor plan, the cut plane is often around door and window head height. If the cut plane is too low or too high, windows, high-level objects, or low-level elements may not display as expected. When troubleshooting a plan, always check the view range before assuming the model is wrong. Family Cut Behaviour ¶ Different Revit categories respond to the cut plane in different ways. This is why two elements at the same height can display differently in the same view. Walls usually cut when the cut plane passes through them, showing their wall build-up and cut lineweight. Doors and windows are hosted by walls and usually display according to the wall opening, family geometry, sill height, and cut plane relationship. Furniture is normally not cut in plan; it usually displays as projection geometry. Casework can behave more like furniture or more like model geometry depending on how the family is built. Generic models depend heavily on their family category, geometry, and visibility settings, so they are common sources of visibility confusion. When an object does not display as expected, check its category, family visibility settings, host relationship, and height relative to the view range. Plan Regions and Underlays ¶ A plan region allows part of a plan view to use a different view range from the rest of the view. This is useful for split-level areas, stairs, mezzanines, high windows, or local conditions where the standard floor plan cut plane does not show the necessary information. Underlays let learners see another level or view reference beneath the current plan. They are useful for coordination and comparison, but they should not be confused with live visible model geometry in the active view. Use underlays temporarily to understand relationships between levels, then turn them off or control them carefully in production views. Checklist ¶ [ ] I can use Visibility/Graphics overrides. [ ] I can distinguish temporary and permanent hide. [ ] I can set detail level and visual style. [ ] I can explain the relationship between categories, families, types, and instances. [ ] I can use category, type, and instance checks when troubleshooting visibility. [ ] I can create and apply a view template. [ ] I can explain how top, cut plane, bottom, and view depth affect a plan. [ ] I can use plan regions for local view range exceptions. [ ] I can troubleshoot why an element is not visible. [ ] I can control underlays and view range. [ ] I can create 3D views, camera views, and duplicated view variants. Homework ¶ Create one working view and one presentation view. Write down three visibility checks to try when an element disappears. Revit Help Links ¶ Visibility and graphics View range View templates 3D views and section boxes Underlays

Explain scale management, referencing drafting views, and office detail library workflows. Demonstrate detail lines, filled regions, masking regions, detail components, and insulation. Discuss safe CAD linking workflows and why exploding imported CAD can damage model performance. 2D Detail Component Families ¶ Detail components are 2D annotation families used in drafting views and detail views. They are useful for repeated detail items such as people, fixings, brackets, insulation symbols, or standard construction components that do not need to be modelled in 3D. To introduce the workflow, create a simple detail component family from a DWG reference: Start from a detail component family template. Import or link the DWG as a tracing reference. Draw clean Revit linework over the useful geometry. Add filled regions or masking regions where needed. Add a yes/no visibility parameter to control an optional part of the component. Load the detail component into the project and place it in a drafting view. The important lesson is that office detail libraries should be made from clean Revit annotation elements where possible. Imported CAD can be useful as a starting point, but it should not become uncontrolled linework scattered through the project. Linking a Facade Detail ¶ When using an external facade detail, prefer linking the CAD file into a controlled drafting view rather than importing and exploding it. A linked file can be reloaded, managed, and removed more safely. If the detail needs to become office-standard Revit content, trace or rebuild the necessary parts using Revit detail lines, filled regions, masking regions, and detail components. docs.text: Detail components are 2D annotation families used in drafting views and detail views. They are useful for repeated detail items such as people, fixings, brackets, insulation symbols, or standard construction components that do not need to be modelled in 3D. To introduce the workflow, create a simple detail component family from a DWG reference: Start from a detail component family template. Import or link the DWG as a tracing reference. Draw clean Revit linework over the useful geometry. Add filled regions or masking regions where needed. Add a yes/no visibility parameter to control an optional part of the component. Load the detail component into the project and place it in a drafting view. The important lesson is that office detail libraries should be made from clean Revit annotation elements where possible. Imported CAD can be useful as a starting point, but it should not become uncontrolled linework scattered through the project.

docs.text: When using an external facade detail, prefer linking the CAD file into a controlled drafting view rather than importing and exploding it. A linked file can be reloaded, managed, and removed more safely.
